clue.text: Responsibility parson usually embraces

indicators.note: the phrase parson usually holds the answer within it, straddling the two words

explanation.surface: A vicar's routine duties are under discussion.
explanation.walkthrough: 'embraces' tells you the answer sits inside 'parson usually', across the join between the words.
explanation.definitionFit: A burden or duty that falls on someone is their responsibility, a direct synonym.

clue.text: Amusement caused by it in the course of Spring term at Oxford

indicators.note: something placed in the course of another lies within it, so one piece goes inside the other

parts.note: Hilary is the name of Oxford University's term running from January to Easter
taken as written

explanation.surface: Laughter breaks out among students during the early-year session at Oxford.
explanation.walkthrough: Oxford University names its three terms Michaelmas, Hilary and Trinity; the one after Christmas counts as the spring term. 'in the course of' signals the insertion.
explanation.definitionFit: Hilarity is great merriment or laughter, a synonym for amusement.

clue.text: Jargon used in shelled hospital in the wars

indicators.note: someone in the wars is knocked about, so the remaining letters are battered into a new order
removing the shell takes away the outer letters of the word hospital

explanation.surface: Military slang is overheard in a field hospital under bombardment.
explanation.walkthrough: 'shelled' strips the outer letters H and L from hospital, leaving OSPITA; 'in the wars' rearranges those six letters. 'Shelled' reads as bombarded, fitting the war picture.
explanation.definitionFit: Patois is a local dialect or the special speech of a group, close in sense to jargon.

clue.text: Working wife paying separately

parts.note: a machine that is going is working or running
'my old Dutch' is Cockney slang for one's wife

explanation.surface: A married couple with two incomes split every bill.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Dutch' for wife comes from Cockney rhyming slang, 'Duchess of Fife' shortened, as in the music-hall song 'My Old Dutch'.
explanation.definitionFit: Going Dutch is the idiom for each person paying their own share of a bill.

clue.text: Assure clubs about company

parts.note: C is the card-suit abbreviation for clubs
on means about or concerning, as in a book on birds
a firm is a business company

explanation.surface: A golf or card club gives guarantees about a business.
explanation.definitionFit: To confirm something is to make it certain or assure someone of it.

clue.text: Instrument found in small room by orchestra's leader

parts.note: a cell is a small room, as in a prison or monastery

indicators.note: the leader of a word is its first letter, here of orchestra's

explanation.surface: An instrument is discovered in a tiny practice room by the first violinist.
explanation.definitionFit: The cello is a large bowed string instrument played in orchestras.

clue.text: Hallucinogen, marvellous to shoot up

parts.note: magic is used informally to mean wonderful or marvellous
to mushroom is to grow or spring up rapidly

explanation.surface: A drug user praises the thrill of injecting.
explanation.walkthrough: 'shoot up' looks like drug slang for injecting, but here it means to grow fast.
explanation.definitionFit: Certain fungi containing psilocybin are taken as a drug that causes hallucinations.

clue.text: Steer clear of a vacuum

parts.note: taken as written
a void is an empty space or vacuum

explanation.surface: Advice to keep away from an empty space, or perhaps a vacuum cleaner.
explanation.definitionFit: To avoid something is to keep away from it, a direct synonym.

clue.text: Certificate ambassador detailed

indicators.note: read as de-tailed: the word loses its tail, its final letter

parts.note: an ambassador is a diplomat

explanation.surface: An envoy's credentials are set out in full.
explanation.walkthrough: 'detailed' looks like 'in detail' but means de-tailed: DIPLOMAT loses its last letter T.
explanation.definitionFit: A diploma is a certificate awarded for completing a course of study.

clue.text: Quiet monk installing small sort of screen

parts.note: p (piano) is the musical marking for quiet

indicators.note: the monk installs a letter, taking it inside himself

parts.note: a lama is a Buddhist monk in Tibet
S is the clothing abbreviation for small

explanation.surface: A silent monk sets up a little television.
explanation.walkthrough: 'installing' puts S inside LAMA, giving LASMA, after P.
explanation.definitionFit: Plasma screens are a type of flat-panel television display.

clue.text: Adults in classes describing heartless women

indicators.note: to describe a shape is to draw around it, so one piece encircles the other

parts.note: groups are classes or categories

indicators.note: a heartless word loses its middle, keeping only its first and last letters

explanation.surface: Grown people in lessons talk about cruel women.
explanation.walkthrough: 'heartless' leaves W and N of women, which 'describing' puts inside GROUPS.
explanation.definitionFit: Grown-ups is the informal word for adults, especially used by or to children.

clue.text: Struck by love, men fall apart

parts.note: got can mean hit or struck, as in the bullet got him
love is zero in tennis, shown as the letter O
chessmen are called pieces

explanation.surface: Smitten with romance, the men lose their composure.
explanation.walkthrough: 'men' looks like people but means the pieces in chess or draughts.
explanation.definitionFit: To go to pieces is the idiom for losing control or breaking down emotionally.

clue.text: Old hotel when refurbished, all in all

indicators.note: something refurbished is done up again, so these letters are rebuilt in a fresh order

explanation.surface: An ageing hotel was renovated at some point, overall.
explanation.walkthrough: 'refurbished' signals the anagram; the surface pictures a renovated hotel, but the definition is the closing phrase meaning overall.
explanation.definitionFit: Both phrases mean taking everything into account, generally speaking.

clue.text: Carry out order causing catastrophe

parts.note: to do something is to carry it out
OM is the Order of Merit, a British honour

explanation.surface: Following a command leads to disaster.
explanation.walkthrough: 'order' is an honour here, the Order of Merit, not a command.
explanation.definitionFit: Doom is ruin or a terrible fate, close in sense to catastrophe.

clue.text: Your drink: I don't care for it

definitions.meaning: a beverage that is yours, and so playfully not mine
the idiom for something one does not like

explanation.surface: Handing someone back their beverage with a sniff of dislike.
explanation.walkthrough: The first reading is literal: if it's your drink, it is not mine.
explanation.definitionFit: The idiom says something is not to one's taste, literally a cup of tea belonging to someone else.

clue.text: Highly-strung member of the Crazy Gang (American)

parts.note: Jimmy Nervo was one of the Crazy Gang, a British comedy troupe of the 1930s to 1950s

explanation.surface: One of a famous comic troupe, from America, is tense.
explanation.walkthrough: The Crazy Gang were a British music-hall comedy group; Nervo of the double act Nervo and Knox was one.
explanation.definitionFit: Someone nervous is anxious and easily agitated, as is a highly-strung person.

clue.text: Casually mention drop of tanning lotion

indicators.note: done casually, without care, so the letters fall into a loose new order
a drop of something is a tiny amount, here the first letter of tanning

explanation.surface: Someone offhandedly refers to a dab of sun cream.
explanation.walkthrough: 'drop of' gives T from tanning; 'Casually' rearranges MENTION with that T.
explanation.definitionFit: An ointment is a soothing cream or lotion applied to the skin.

clue.text: Release without charge

definitions.meaning: to let go or set loose, a verb

explanation.surface: A prisoner set loose with no case against them.
explanation.definitionFit: The word means both to let go and costing nothing.

clue.text: Responsible for factory worker being late

parts.note: to be behind something is to be its cause or responsible for it
a hand is a manual worker, as in factory hand

explanation.surface: A factory worker is blamed for poor timekeeping.
explanation.definitionFit: Behindhand means late or behind schedule, especially in payments or work.

clue.text: Piece of furniture in office

definitions.meaning: an agency or department, as in a news agency

explanation.surface: A desk in a workplace.
explanation.definitionFit: The word names both a writing desk and an agency or department.

clue.text: Near end of flight in the dark

parts.note: nigh is an old word for near

indicators.note: the end of a word is its final letter, here of flight

explanation.surface: Approaching the close of a journey after sunset.
explanation.definitionFit: Night is the time of darkness between sunset and sunrise.

clue.text: Don Juan mixed up 'Hair' and 'Loot'

indicators.note: letters mixed up are jumbled into a different arrangement

explanation.surface: Someone confuses the titles of two shows, a musical and a comic play.
explanation.walkthrough: 'mixed up' rearranges HAIR and LOOT. Hair is a rock musical and Loot a Joe Orton farce.
explanation.definitionFit: A Lothario is a seducer of women, after a character in Rowe's play, just like a Don Juan.

clue.text: Handle husband with maturity

parts.note: man is an old word for husband, as in man and wife
age can mean maturity, the state of being grown up

explanation.surface: Coping with a husband who has grown older.
explanation.definitionFit: To manage something is to handle or deal with it.

clue.text: Annoy Noah, initially, on his ship

indicators.note: initially picks the first letter of the word Noah

parts.note: Noah's vessel was the Ark

explanation.surface: Irritating Noah aboard his famous boat.
explanation.walkthrough: To nark is British slang for to irritate.
explanation.definitionFit: Nark is a British informal verb meaning to annoy or irritate.

clue.text: Saucy dance?

parts.note: a dance whose name is also that of a spicy Mexican sauce, read as saucy in the literal sense

explanation.surface: A cheeky, risqué bit of dancing.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Saucy' suggests cheeky, but read literally it means sauce-like.
explanation.definitionFit: Salsa is both a Latin American dance and a tomato-based sauce.

clue.text: Remain uneasy heading for the Tower?

indicators.note: uneasy suggests disturbance, so the letters of remain are unsettled into a new order
the heading of a word is its first letter, here of the

explanation.surface: Staying anxious while making for the Tower of London.
explanation.walkthrough: 'uneasy' rearranges REMAIN into MINARE; 'heading for' takes T from 'the'. 'the Tower' suggests London's, but the definition is just Tower.
explanation.definitionFit: A minaret is a slender tower of a mosque, an example of a tower, hence the question mark.
